bicep.summary: This finding means a nested deployment has debug logging enabled at a level that captures full request or response content, which may include secrets.
bicep.whyFlagged: A Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource has debugSetting.detailLevel set to 'RequestContent', 'ResponseContent', or 'All', logging full HTTP payloads that may contain sensitive data.
bicep.riskImpact: Debug logs with request/response content are stored in Azure deployment history in plain text. These logs may capture secrets, passwords, and access keys, which are accessible to any principal with read access to the resource group.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Set debugSetting.detailLevel to 'None' on all nested Microsoft.Resources/deployments resources, or remove the debugSetting property entirely. Never use 'RequestContent', 'ResponseContent', or 'All' in production deployments.

bicep.name: ARM Template Parameter Data Types
bicep.description: Parameter default values must match the declared parameter type to prevent silent type coercion errors during deployment.
bicep.summary: This finding means a parameter's default value does not match its declared type, which can cause unpredictable deployment behavior.
bicep.whyFlagged: A parameter declares a type (e.g., 'int', 'bool') but its defaultValue is of a different type (e.g., a string '5' for an int parameter).
bicep.riskImpact: Type mismatches in default values can silently accept wrong inputs or cause cryptic deployment failures, making it harder to diagnose and correct insecure configurations.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Ensure each parameter's defaultValue matches its declared type. Use 0 for int defaults, true/false for bool, empty string ('') for string, and [] for array. In Bicep the compiler enforces this at build time.

examples.bad:
// Bicep — type mismatch: int parameter with string default
param retentionDays int = '30'  // String assigned to int

bicep.name: ARM Template Parameter Strong Type
bicep.description: Parameters that reference Azure-specific values should use strong types or allowed-value constraints to prevent invalid inputs.
bicep.summary: This finding means a parameter is missing strong type metadata or allowed-value constraints, allowing any string value to be passed without validation.
bicep.whyFlagged: Parameters for Azure locations, VM SKUs, or other enumerable Azure values are missing metadata.strongType hints or @allowed() constraints, bypassing IDE and toolchain validation.
bicep.riskImpact: Without strong type constraints, operators can pass any string value, increasing the risk of deploying to non-compliant regions, using deprecated SKUs, or referencing non-existent resources.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Use @allowed() decorators in Bicep to constrain parameters to a known set of valid values (e.g., permitted regions or SKUs). For ARM, add metadata.strongType to enable Azure Portal dropdowns and validation.

examples.bad:
// Bicep — unrestricted location parameter
param location string = resourceGroup().location  // Accepts any string

bicep.name: ARM Template Expression Length
bicep.description: ARM template expressions must not exceed the Azure-imposed maximum expression length to avoid deployment failures.
bicep.summary: This finding means a template expression exceeds the maximum length limit, which will cause the deployment to fail.
bicep.whyFlagged: A template expression exceeds the ARM engine's maximum supported expression length of 24,576 characters.
bicep.riskImpact: Expressions exceeding the limit cause deployment failures. Overly complex expressions also reduce maintainability and increase the likelihood of logic errors in security-relevant computations such as naming or RBAC assignments.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Refactor long expressions by splitting them into multiple intermediate variables in the 'variables' section and referencing those variables. Consider migrating complex expressions to Bicep, which produces more concise compiled ARM output.

bicep.name: ARM Template Parameter File Valid
bicep.description: ARM template parameter files must be valid JSON conforming to the parameter file schema.
bicep.summary: This finding means the parameter file contains malformed JSON or violates the parameter file schema, which can cause silent fallback to insecure default values.
bicep.whyFlagged: The parameter file is not valid JSON, or is missing required fields such as $schema, contentVersion, or the parameters object.
bicep.riskImpact: Invalid parameter files cause deployment failures or silent fallback to template default values, which may be insecure test-oriented defaults not suitable for production.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Ensure parameter files are valid JSON containing $schema (set to the parameter file schema URL), contentVersion, and a parameters object. Validate using 'az deployment group validate' or arm-ttk before every deployment.

bicep.name: ARM Template Parameter File HTTPS Scheme
bicep.description: ARM template parameter file schema URIs must use the HTTPS scheme rather than HTTP.
bicep.summary: This finding means the parameter file $schema URL uses HTTP, exposing toolchain schema validation to potential interception.
bicep.whyFlagged: The $schema property in the parameter file starts with 'http://' rather than 'https://'.
bicep.riskImpact: HTTP schema references in parameter files may be intercepted during toolchain validation, potentially allowing a malicious schema to suppress warnings or permit dangerous parameter values.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Change the $schema URL in the parameter file from 'http://' to 'https://'. Example: replace 'http://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2019-04-01/deploymentParameters.json#' with the https equivalent.

bicep.name: ARM Template Metadata Link
bicep.description: ARM template parameter files should include a metadata link pointing to the corresponding ARM template file.
bicep.summary: This finding means the parameter file is missing a metadata.template link, making it unclear which template this parameter file belongs to.
bicep.whyFlagged: The parameter file has no metadata.template property that links it back to its parent ARM template file.
bicep.riskImpact: Without a metadata link, operators or automation pipelines may pair the wrong parameter file with a template, silently applying incorrect security configurations to production deployments.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Add a metadata property with a template field to the parameter file pointing to the relative path of the corresponding ARM template. Example: add '"metadata": { "template": "../azuredeploy.json" }' at the top level of the parameter file.

bicep.name: ARM Template Parameter Value Set
bicep.description: Parameter files should provide explicit values for all template parameters rather than silently relying on template-defined defaults.
bicep.summary: This finding means the parameter file does not specify values for some parameters, which will cause the deployment to fall back to template default values that may be insecure.
bicep.whyFlagged: One or more parameters defined in the corresponding ARM template have no entry in the parameter file, meaning the deployment will use the template's default values.
bicep.riskImpact: Template default values are often set to permissive or test-oriented values. Silently falling back to defaults in production can result in insecure configurations such as wide-open NSG rules, disabled encryption, or development SKUs.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Provide explicit values for all parameters in the parameter file, even those that have safe-looking defaults. Use Azure Key Vault parameter references for all sensitive values. Review default values in templates periodically to ensure they remain secure.

references.name: Azure Key Vault in Parameter Files

bicep.name: ARM Template Use Comments
bicep.description: ARM template resource definitions should include a 'comments' property documenting the purpose of each resource.
bicep.summary: This finding means resource blocks in the ARM template lack comments, reducing auditability and slowing down security reviews.
bicep.whyFlagged: ARM template resource objects do not include a 'comments' field to explain their purpose, security role, or relationship to other resources.
bicep.riskImpact: Without comments, security reviewers and incident responders cannot quickly determine the intent of individual resources. This increases the time needed for security audits and the chance of overlooking misconfigured resources.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Add a 'comments' property to each resource object in ARM JSON templates. In Bicep, add inline // comments above each resource declaration explaining its security role and dependencies.

bicep.name: ARM Template Use Descriptions
bicep.description: Bicep resources, modules, and parameters should include @description() decorators to communicate purpose in the compiled ARM template.
bicep.summary: This finding means Bicep declarations are missing @description() decorators, so the compiled ARM template has no metadata descriptions for reviewers.
bicep.whyFlagged: Bicep resource, module, or parameter declarations do not have @description() decorators, resulting in generated ARM templates with no documentation metadata.
bicep.riskImpact: Without descriptions in the compiled template, operators relying on the ARM JSON cannot understand resource purposes, increasing the risk of misconfiguration during manual edits and slowing down security reviews.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Add @description() decorators to all Bicep resource, module, and parameter declarations. These compile into metadata.description fields in the generated ARM template and are also surfaced in the Azure Portal and tooling.

bicep.name: Deployment Output Secret Value
bicep.description: Deployment outputs must not expose secret or secure parameter values that would be visible in deployment history.
bicep.summary: This finding means a deployment output exposes a sensitive value such as a password, connection string, or key, making it visible in Azure deployment history to anyone with read access.
bicep.whyFlagged: The template outputs section references a securestring parameter, a Key Vault secret, or a resource property known to contain sensitive data (e.g., administratorLoginPassword, primaryKey).
bicep.riskImpact: Deployment outputs are stored in plain text in Azure deployment history indefinitely. Any principal with Reader access to the resource group can retrieve exposed secrets, leading to credential theft and potential full environment compromise.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Remove sensitive values from deployment outputs entirely. If a downstream resource needs the value, pass it as a secure parameter directly rather than routing it through an output. Mark any necessary output types as securestring to prevent storage in deployment history.

bicep.name: Deployment Admin Username Hardcoded
bicep.description: Administrator username properties must not be set from hardcoded or deterministic values; they must come from secure parameters.
bicep.summary: This finding means the template sets an administrator username from a hardcoded string or predictable expression, making it trivially discoverable by attackers.
bicep.whyFlagged: An administratorLogin or similar admin username property is set to a literal string (e.g., 'admin', 'adminUser') or a deterministic expression rather than a secure parameter supplied at deployment time.
bicep.riskImpact: Hardcoded admin usernames are easily discovered and used in brute-force, credential stuffing, and targeted attacks against management interfaces. Using known usernames like 'admin' or 'sa' significantly reduces the work factor for attackers.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Replace hardcoded admin usernames with a parameter decorated with @secure() (Bicep) or type securestring (ARM). Supply the value via a Key Vault reference in the parameter file or through a CI/CD pipeline secret. Avoid predictable usernames such as 'admin', 'administrator', 'root', or 'sa'.

bicep.name: Deployment Secure Value
bicep.description: Resource properties that hold sensitive values must be sourced from secure parameters, not plain string parameters or hardcoded literals.
bicep.summary: This finding means a secret property (password, key, connection string) is set from a non-secure parameter or literal, causing it to appear in plain text in deployment history.
bicep.whyFlagged: A property known to hold sensitive data (e.g., administratorLoginPassword, primarySharedKey) is assigned from a plain 'string' type parameter or a hardcoded literal instead of a @secure() parameter.
bicep.riskImpact: Plain string parameters are stored in Azure deployment history in clear text. Any principal with Reader access to the resource group can retrieve exposed secrets from deployment history, enabling unauthorized access to databases, storage, and other resources.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Mark all parameters that carry sensitive data with @secure() in Bicep or type securestring/secureObject in ARM. Supply values via Azure Key Vault parameter references in the deployment parameter file. Never embed secrets as literal values in templates or parameter files.

references.name: Azure Key Vault References in Parameters

bicep.name: Deployment Outer Secret Leak
bicep.description: Nested deployments must use inner scope expression evaluation to prevent secure parameter values from being evaluated in the parent context and logged.
bicep.summary: This finding means a nested deployment uses outer scope expression evaluation, causing secure parameters to be resolved in the parent deployment context where they may appear in logs.
bicep.whyFlagged: A Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource has expressionEvaluationOptions.scope set to 'Outer', or omits the property in a context that defaults to outer evaluation, allowing secure parameters to leak into the parent deployment history.
bicep.riskImpact: Outer scope evaluation resolves secure parameters in the parent deployment context. Resolved secret values may then appear in parent deployment logs and history in plain text, accessible to any principal with read access to the resource group.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Set expressionEvaluationOptions.scope to 'Inner' on all nested Microsoft.Resources/deployments resources. Inner scope ensures secure parameters are evaluated entirely within the nested deployment context and are never surfaced to the parent deployment history.

bicep.name: Deployment Secure Parameter
bicep.description: Parameters whose names or usage indicate they carry sensitive data must be declared as securestring or secureObject.
bicep.summary: This finding means the template contains parameters with names suggesting sensitive content (password, secret, key, token) that are not typed as secure parameters.
bicep.whyFlagged: Parameters with names matching patterns such as 'password', 'secret', 'key', 'token', 'credential', or 'connectionString' are declared as plain 'string' type rather than 'securestring'.
bicep.riskImpact: Plain string parameters are stored unredacted in Azure deployment history. Any principal with read access to the resource group can view these values, enabling credential theft and unauthorized access to resources provisioned by the template.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Declare all parameters holding sensitive data with @secure() in Bicep or type securestring/secureObject in ARM. Review all parameter names for indicators of sensitive content and audit existing deployment history to assess exposure of already-deployed templates.

bicep.name: Deployment Naming Requirements
bicep.description: Nested deployment resource names must meet Azure naming requirements: 1–64 characters, valid characters only, and must not end with a period.
bicep.summary: This finding means a nested deployment resource name violates Azure naming rules, which can cause deployment failures or naming conflicts in deployment history.
bicep.whyFlagged: The name of a Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource contains invalid characters, exceeds 64 characters, ends with a period, or is empty.
bicep.riskImpact: Invalid deployment names cause hard-to-diagnose deployment failures. Inconsistent naming also reduces auditability and makes it harder to trace security-relevant deployments through logs and history.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Ensure all nested deployment names are 1–64 characters, use only alphanumerics, underscores, parentheses, hyphens, and periods, and do not end with a period. Adopt a consistent naming convention such as 'deploy-<module>-<environment>' for easier auditing.

bicep.name: Deployment Secret Leak
bicep.description: All template parameters carrying sensitive data must be marked as secure to prevent secrets from being written to deployment history and logs.
bicep.summary: This finding means one or more parameters that receive sensitive values are not marked as secure, causing those values to be stored unredacted in Azure deployment history.
bicep.whyFlagged: The scanner identified parameters that receive sensitive values—based on name patterns or their assignment to sensitive resource properties—that are not typed as securestring or secureObject.
bicep.riskImpact: Azure deployment history retains non-secure parameter values in plain text for the lifetime of the deployment record. Compromised identities or overly permissive service principals with read access to the resource group can retrieve all exposed secrets, enabling lateral movement and resource takeover.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Audit all template parameters for sensitive content. Mark them with @secure() in Bicep or securestring/secureObject type in ARM. Rotate any credentials that were already passed as plain parameters in previous deployments. Use Azure Key Vault references for all production secrets. Consider running 'az deployment operation list' to review what has already been logged.

references.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1552.001: Credentials in Files
Azure Key Vault References in Parameters

bicep.name: Deployment Script Pinned URL
bicep.description: Deployment scripts that reference external script URLs must pin to a specific immutable version to prevent supply chain attacks.
bicep.summary: This finding means a deployment script resource loads an external script from an unpinned URL, making the deployment vulnerable to supply chain tampering.
bicep.whyFlagged: A Microsoft.Resources/deploymentScripts resource references an external script URL pointing to a mutable reference such as a 'main' branch, 'latest' tag, or floating URL that can be changed by a third party.
bicep.riskImpact: Deployment scripts run with managed identity permissions. An attacker who compromises the hosting endpoint (e.g., a GitHub repository or CDN) can inject malicious code that executes arbitrary Azure API calls, exfiltrates secrets, creates backdoor role assignments, or destroys resources.
bicep.remediationGuidance: Pin external script URLs to a specific immutable commit SHA or content hash. Prefer storing scripts in a private Azure Blob Storage container with a SAS token or using inline scripts via the scriptContent property to eliminate external URL dependencies entirely. Add URL integrity checks if external URLs must be used.

references.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1195: Supply Chain Compromise

ansible.name: uri: Certificate Validation Enabled
ansible.description: The uri module is called with validate_certs: false, disabling TLS certificate verification.
ansible.summary: Disabling certificate validation in the uri module allows man-in-the-middle attacks on HTTPS requests made by the playbook.
ansible.whyFlagged: validate_certs: false tells Ansible to skip verification of the remote server's SSL/TLS certificate, making the connection vulnerable to interception.
ansible.riskImpact: An attacker positioned between the Ansible controller and the remote host can intercept or modify traffic, potentially injecting malicious content or harvesting credentials.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove validate_certs: false or set it to true. If the server uses a private CA, supply the CA certificate via the ca_path option instead of disabling validation.

ansible.name: get_url: Certificate Validation Enabled
ansible.description: The get_url module is called with validate_certs: false, disabling TLS certificate verification when downloading files.
ansible.summary: Disabling certificate validation allows downloaded files to be silently replaced by malicious content.
ansible.whyFlagged: validate_certs: false skips TLS verification for the file download, enabling interception.
ansible.riskImpact: A malicious actor can substitute the downloaded file with a tampered version, leading to supply chain compromise on managed hosts.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set validate_certs: true and ensure the remote server's certificate is trusted. Use a checksum parameter to verify file integrity.

examples.bad:
- get_url:
    url: https://example.com/file.tar.gz
    dest: /tmp/file.tar.gz
    validate_certs: false
examples.good:
- get_url:
    url: https://example.com/file.tar.gz
    dest: /tmp/file.tar.gz
    validate_certs: true
    checksum: sha256:abc123...

ansible.name: yum: Certificate Validation Enabled
ansible.description: The yum module is called with validate_certs: false, disabling SSL certificate validation for the package manager.
ansible.summary: Skipping certificate validation with yum allows repository metadata and packages to be tampered with in transit.
ansible.whyFlagged: validate_certs: false removes a layer of supply-chain protection when communicating with RPM repositories.
ansible.riskImpact: Malicious packages can be injected into the package installation flow, resulting in arbitrary code execution on managed hosts.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove validate_certs: false. Ensure the yum repository is served over HTTPS and the CA certificate is trusted on the managed host.

ansible.name: yum: SSL Verification Enabled
ansible.description: The yum module is called with sslverify: false, disabling SSL peer verification.
ansible.summary: sslverify: false removes TLS verification for yum repository connections, exposing package downloads to interception.
ansible.whyFlagged: This setting instructs the underlying yum/dnf tooling to skip SSL peer verification for the configured repository.
ansible.riskImpact: Attackers can intercept repository communication and serve malicious package metadata or RPM files.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove sslverify: false. If using a private internal repository, configure its CA certificate in /etc/pki/ca-trust instead.

ansible.name: apt: Reject Unauthenticated Packages
ansible.description: The apt module is called with allow_unauthenticated: true, permitting installation of packages with untrusted or missing GPG signatures.
ansible.summary: Allowing unauthenticated apt packages undermines Debian/Ubuntu's package signing protections.
ansible.whyFlagged: allow_unauthenticated: true bypasses GPG signature checks, accepting packages regardless of whether they have been tampered with.
ansible.riskImpact: Malicious or tampered .deb packages can be installed silently, leading to persistent compromise of the managed host.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove allow_unauthenticated: true. Import the repository's GPG key with apt_key and use signed repositories only.

ansible.name: apt: force/force_yes Must Not Be Used
ansible.description: The apt module is called with force: true or force_yes: true, which bypasses GPG signature and dependency validation.
ansible.summary: Force-installing packages disables apt's signature and dependency checks, bypassing key security controls.
ansible.whyFlagged: force/force_yes instructs apt to proceed even when packages fail signature checks or conflict with existing packages.
ansible.riskImpact: Tampered or malicious packages can be forcefully installed, resulting in code execution, privilege escalation, or system instability.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove force: true and force_yes: true. Resolve dependency conflicts or import the missing GPG key instead.

ansible.name: uri: Use HTTPS URL
ansible.description: The uri module is making a request to an HTTP (non-HTTPS) URL, transmitting data in plaintext.
ansible.summary: HTTP URLs in the uri module expose request and response data to passive eavesdropping and active interception.
ansible.whyFlagged: The url parameter does not start with https://, meaning the connection is unencrypted.
ansible.riskImpact: Sensitive data, credentials, or response content can be read or modified by any party with access to the network path.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Change the url to use https:// and ensure the target server has a valid TLS certificate.

ansible.name: get_url: Use HTTPS URL
ansible.description: The get_url module is downloading from an HTTP URL, exposing the transfer to tampering.
ansible.summary: Downloading files over HTTP provides no integrity or confidentiality protection.
ansible.whyFlagged: The url parameter does not use https://, leaving the file download vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.
ansible.riskImpact: The downloaded file can be silently replaced with a malicious payload, leading to arbitrary code execution on the managed host.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Use an https:// URL and add a checksum parameter to verify file integrity after download.

examples.good:
- get_url:
    url: https://example.com/file.tar.gz
    dest: /tmp/file.tar.gz
    checksum: sha256:abc123...

ansible.name: Block: Rescue Section Required
ansible.description: An Ansible block statement does not have an accompanying rescue section to handle task failures.
ansible.summary: Blocks without rescue sections can leave managed hosts in a partially configured or broken state when tasks fail.
ansible.whyFlagged: A block without rescue means any failure inside the block goes unhandled, potentially leaving security-relevant configuration in a half-applied state.
ansible.riskImpact: Unhandled failures during security hardening tasks (firewall rules, user creation, certificate installation) can leave the host in a degraded or insecure state.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Add a rescue section to every block that contains tasks with failure consequences. Use the always section for cleanup that must run regardless.

examples.bad:
- block:
    - name: install package
      apt:
        name: openssl
examples.good:
- block:
    - name: install package
      apt:
        name: openssl
  rescue:
    - name: handle failure
      debug:
        msg: 'Installation failed'

ansible.name: dnf: GPG Check Must Not Be Disabled
ansible.description: The dnf module is called with disable_gpg_check: true, bypassing RPM package signature verification.
ansible.summary: Disabling GPG checks for dnf removes the primary mechanism for verifying that installed packages have not been tampered with.
ansible.whyFlagged: disable_gpg_check: true instructs dnf to install packages without verifying their GPG signatures.
ansible.riskImpact: Unsigned or maliciously signed RPM packages can be installed, enabling persistent compromise of the managed host.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove disable_gpg_check: true. Import the repository's GPG key with rpm_key and use gpgcheck=1 in the repository configuration.

ansible.name: dnf: SSL Verification Enabled
ansible.description: The dnf module is called with sslverify: false, disabling SSL verification for repository communication.
ansible.summary: Disabling SSL verification for dnf exposes repository metadata downloads to tampering.
ansible.whyFlagged: sslverify: false removes TLS peer verification when dnf communicates with the configured repository server.
ansible.riskImpact: Attackers can intercept or replace repository metadata, directing the host to install malicious packages.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove sslverify: false and ensure the repository CA certificate is trusted by the managed host.

ansible.name: dnf: Certificate Validation Enabled
ansible.description: The dnf module is called with validate_certs: false, disabling TLS certificate validation.
ansible.summary: Skipping certificate validation for dnf removes protection against man-in-the-middle attacks on package downloads.
ansible.whyFlagged: validate_certs: false instructs dnf to skip TLS certificate verification for repository connections.
ansible.riskImpact: Package metadata and binaries can be replaced in transit, resulting in installation of malicious software.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove validate_certs: false. Configure the repository to use a properly trusted certificate.

ansible.name: EC2: No Public IP Assignment
ansible.description: An ec2_instance or amazon.aws.ec2_instance task assigns a public IP address to the instance.
ansible.summary: Assigning a public IP directly to an EC2 instance exposes it to the internet without requiring a load balancer or NAT gateway.
ansible.whyFlagged: assign_public_ip: true (or network.assign_public_ip: true) makes the EC2 instance directly reachable from the public internet.
ansible.riskImpact: Publicly accessible instances have a larger attack surface. Any unpatched service or misconfigured firewall can be exploited directly from the internet.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Do not assign public IPs to instances. Place instances in private subnets and use a NAT gateway or load balancer for outbound and inbound traffic respectively.

examples.bad:
- ec2_instance:
    name: my-server
    network:
      assign_public_ip: true
examples.good:
- ec2_instance:
    name: my-server
    network:
      assign_public_ip: false

ansible.name: EC2: EBS Optimization Enabled
ansible.description: An ec2_instance task does not explicitly enable EBS optimization (ebs_optimized: true).
ansible.summary: EBS-optimized instances provide dedicated bandwidth to Amazon EBS I/O, preventing resource contention.
ansible.whyFlagged: ebs_optimized is absent or set to false, meaning EBS I/O shares bandwidth with other traffic.
ansible.riskImpact: Without dedicated EBS bandwidth, I/O performance can degrade under load and contention could be leveraged by a noisy-neighbour attack.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set ebs_optimized: true in the ec2_instance task. Verify the chosen instance type supports EBS optimization.

examples.good:
- ec2_instance:
    name: my-server
    instance_type: t3.medium
    ebs_optimized: true

ansible.name: PANOS: Management Profile Must Not Allow HTTP
ansible.description: A panos_management_profile task enables plain-text HTTP management access (http: true).
ansible.summary: Enabling HTTP on a PAN-OS Interface Management Profile allows credentials and management traffic to be transmitted in cleartext.
ansible.whyFlagged: http: true enables unencrypted HTTP access to the management interface.
ansible.riskImpact: Cleartext HTTP exposes credentials and session tokens to network eavesdroppers and enables session hijacking.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set http: false (or omit the key) and use HTTPS exclusively for management access.

ansible.name: PANOS: Management Profile Must Not Allow Telnet
ansible.description: A panos_management_profile task enables Telnet management access (telnet: true).
ansible.summary: Telnet transmits all data including credentials in plaintext, making it trivially interceptable.
ansible.whyFlagged: telnet: true enables unencrypted Telnet access to the management interface.
ansible.riskImpact: Any attacker on the network path can capture administrator credentials and session data.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set telnet: false (or omit the key) and use SSH for CLI access.

ansible.name: PANOS: DSRI Must Not Be Enabled in Security Policies
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task has disable_server_response_inspection: true.
ansible.summary: DSRI prevents the firewall from inspecting server-to-client traffic, hiding malicious payloads in responses.
ansible.whyFlagged: disable_server_response_inspection: true disables threat inspection on return traffic.
ansible.riskImpact: Malicious content in server responses (e.g. C2 callbacks, data exfiltration) passes through the firewall uninspected.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set disable_server_response_inspection: false or omit the key (false is the default).

ansible.name: PANOS: Security Rules Must Not Use Application 'any'
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task sets application to 'any', bypassing App-ID inspection.
ansible.summary: Allowing any application defeats Palo Alto's App-ID technology and permits unapproved applications through the firewall.
ansible.whyFlagged: application: any (or a list containing 'any') disables application-layer control.
ansible.riskImpact: Unapproved, risky, or malicious applications can traverse the firewall unchecked.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Specify an explicit list of approved application identifiers instead of 'any'.

ansible.name: PANOS: Security Rules Must Not Use Service 'any'
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task sets service to 'any', allowing traffic on all ports and protocols.
ansible.summary: Permitting any service opens all ports and protocols on the rule, significantly widening the attack surface.
ansible.whyFlagged: service: any (or a list containing 'any') removes port/protocol restrictions from the rule.
ansible.riskImpact: Attackers can use non-standard ports and protocols for C2 communication or data exfiltration.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Replace 'any' with specific service objects or use 'application-default' to limit traffic to well-known ports.

ansible.name: PANOS: Security Rules Must Not Have Both Source and Destination IP 'any'
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task has both source_ip and destination_ip set to 'any'.
ansible.summary: Both source and destination IP being 'any' creates an unrestricted rule that defeats the purpose of the firewall.
ansible.whyFlagged: source_ip and destination_ip are both 'any', creating a catch-all rule.
ansible.riskImpact: All traffic matching the application and service criteria is permitted regardless of origin or destination.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Restrict at least one of source_ip or destination_ip to specific addresses, address objects, or address groups.

ansible.name: PANOS: Security Policies Must Have a Description
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task does not include a description field.
ansible.summary: Undocumented firewall rules complicate audits, increase the risk of accidental misconfigurations, and hinder compliance reporting.
ansible.whyFlagged: The description field is absent or empty in the panos_security_rule task.
ansible.riskImpact: Without documentation, stale or overly permissive rules may go unnoticed during reviews.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Add a meaningful description field to each panos_security_rule task explaining the business justification.

examples.good:
- paloaltonetworks.panos.panos_security_rule:
    rule_name: allow-web
    description: 'Allow outbound web browsing for corporate users'

ansible.name: PANOS: Security Policies Must Have a Log Forwarding Profile
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task does not specify a log_forwarding profile.
ansible.summary: Without log forwarding, security events are stored only on the local device and unavailable for centralised SIEM analysis.
ansible.whyFlagged: log_forwarding is absent or empty, meaning traffic logs will not be forwarded externally.
ansible.riskImpact: Security events may be lost and attacks may go undetected if local storage fills up or the device is compromised.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set log_forwarding: <profile_name> in each panos_security_rule task to forward logs to Panorama or an external syslog.

ansible.name: PANOS: Logging at Session End Must Be Enabled
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task has log_end set to false or omitted.
ansible.summary: Session-end logs capture the full traffic summary and are essential for incident investigation and compliance.
ansible.whyFlagged: log_end is false or not set, disabling session-end log generation.
ansible.riskImpact: Without session-end logs, security analysts cannot correlate complete flows during incident response.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set log_end: true in each panos_security_rule task. This is the PAN-OS default; verify it is not explicitly disabled.

ansible.name: PANOS: IPsec Profiles Must Not Use Insecure Authentication Algorithms
ansible.description: A panos_ipsec_profile task specifies an insecure authentication algorithm (MD5 or SHA-1).
ansible.summary: MD5 and SHA-1 are cryptographically broken and susceptible to collision attacks, undermining VPN integrity.
ansible.whyFlagged: The authentication field contains md5 or sha1 which are considered weak algorithms.
ansible.riskImpact: Insecure authentication algorithms can be exploited to forge authentication hashes, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on VPN tunnels.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Replace MD5/SHA-1 with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 in the authentication list.

ansible.name: PANOS: IPsec Profiles Must Not Use Insecure Protocols
ansible.description: A panos_ipsec_profile task specifies an insecure encryption protocol (DES, 3DES, or null).
ansible.summary: DES and 3DES provide inadequate confidentiality for VPN traffic and are deprecated by NIST.
ansible.whyFlagged: The encryption field contains des, 3des, or null which are weak or provide no encryption.
ansible.riskImpact: Weak encryption can be broken by an attacker, exposing all VPN traffic in plaintext.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Replace DES/3DES with AES-128-GCM or AES-256-GCM in the encryption list.

ansible.name: PANOS: Security Zones Must Have a Zone Protection Profile
ansible.description: A panos_zone task does not specify a zone_profile (Zone Protection Profile).
ansible.summary: Without a Zone Protection Profile, the zone is unprotected against flood, reconnaissance, and packet-based attacks.
ansible.whyFlagged: zone_profile is absent or empty in the panos_zone task.
ansible.riskImpact: Zones without protection profiles are vulnerable to SYN/UDP/ICMP flood attacks and packet-based exploits.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Create a Zone Protection Profile in Panorama/PAN-OS and reference it via zone_profile in the panos_zone task.

ansible.name: PANOS: Zone User-ID Must Define an Include ACL
ansible.description: A panos_zone task enables User-ID (enable_userid: true) without defining an include_acl.
ansible.summary: Without an Include ACL, User-ID collects identity from all subnets in the zone, potentially exposing sensitive authentication data.
ansible.whyFlagged: enable_userid is true but include_acl is not defined, meaning User-ID has unrestricted scope.
ansible.riskImpact: User-ID data leakage can expose identity information from subnets that should be excluded from identity-based policy.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set include_acl to the list of subnets that legitimately require User-ID in the panos_zone task.

examples.good:
- paloaltonetworks.panos.panos_zone:
    name: trust
    enable_userid: true
    include_acl: ['10.0.1.0/24']

ansible.name: PANOS: Session-Start Logging Must Be Disabled Except for Troubleshooting
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task has log_start: true, enabling session-start logging.
ansible.summary: Session-start logging doubles log volume and can overwhelm collectors, causing log-loss events that hide genuine security incidents.
ansible.whyFlagged: log_start: true is set on a security rule where it may not be intentional.
ansible.riskImpact: Excessive log volume can cause log-forwarding drops, making incident detection unreliable.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set log_start: false unless specifically needed for troubleshooting a particular rule.

ansible.name: PANOS: Security Rules Must Not Have Both Source and Destination Zone 'any'
ansible.description: A panos_security_rule task has both source_zone and destination_zone set to 'any'.
ansible.summary: A rule with both zones as 'any' matches all inter-zone and intra-zone traffic, creating a universal allow rule.
ansible.whyFlagged: source_zone and destination_zone are both 'any', effectively removing zone-based segmentation.
ansible.riskImpact: Traffic is allowed between all zones, negating network segmentation and allowing lateral movement.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Restrict at least one of source_zone or destination_zone to a specific zone name.

ansible.name: ARM Template File Valid
ansible.description: ARM template files must be valid, well-formed JSON that conforms to the Azure Resource Manager schema.
ansible.summary: This finding means the ARM template file is malformed or missing required top-level fields, preventing reliable deployment.
ansible.whyFlagged: The template file is not valid JSON or is missing required fields such as $schema, contentVersion, or the resources array.
ansible.riskImpact: An invalid template cannot be deployed, causing pipeline failures. Structural errors may mask missing security controls and create inconsistent configurations across environments.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Validate the ARM template using 'az deployment group validate' or the ARM Template Toolkit (arm-ttk). Ensure the file is valid JSON containing a $schema reference, contentVersion, and at least one resource. Prefer authoring in Bicep and compiling with 'bicep build' to generate consistently valid ARM templates.

ansible.name: ARM Template Schema Version
ansible.description: ARM template files must reference a recent version of the Azure Resource Manager schema.
ansible.summary: This finding means the ARM template uses an outdated $schema version that may not support current resource types and security-relevant properties.
ansible.whyFlagged: The $schema field references an old schema version (e.g., 2014-04-01-preview or 2015-01-01) instead of the recommended 2019-04-01 schema.
ansible.riskImpact: Outdated schema versions may silently ignore newer security-relevant properties, causing deployments to appear successful while missing critical configurations.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Update the $schema to 'https://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2019-04-01/deploymentTemplate.json#'. For subscription-scope templates use the 2018-05-01 schema. For management group or tenant scope use the respective newer schemas.

ansible.name: ARM Template Schema HTTPS Scheme
ansible.description: ARM template schema URIs must use the HTTPS scheme rather than HTTP.
ansible.summary: This finding means the ARM template $schema URL uses an insecure HTTP URI, exposing schema validation traffic to interception.
ansible.whyFlagged: The $schema property starts with 'http://' rather than 'https://', which allows toolchain schema downloads over an unencrypted channel.
ansible.riskImpact: HTTP schema references can be intercepted or tampered with by a man-in-the-middle attacker, potentially injecting a malicious schema that suppresses validation warnings for insecure configurations.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Change the $schema URL prefix from 'http://' to 'https://'. This is a one-character fix: replace 'http://schema.management.azure.com/...' with 'https://schema.management.azure.com/...'.

ansible.name: ARM Template Parameter Metadata
ansible.description: Each ARM template parameter should have a metadata description documenting its purpose and expected values.
ansible.summary: This finding means one or more parameters are missing metadata descriptions, reducing auditability and increasing misconfiguration risk.
ansible.whyFlagged: Parameters lack a metadata.description property, making it unclear what values are expected and whether security-sensitive inputs are being passed correctly.
ansible.riskImpact: Without descriptions, operators may supply incorrect values for security-sensitive parameters such as admin credentials, network CIDR ranges, or SKU selections, increasing the risk of insecure deployments.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Add a metadata.description property to every parameter declaration explaining its purpose, expected format, and any security constraints. In Bicep use the @description() decorator above each param declaration.

ansible.name: ARM Template Has Resources
ansible.description: Each ARM template file should deploy at least one resource to ensure the deployment has meaningful effect.
ansible.summary: This finding means the ARM template contains an empty resources array, making the deployment a no-op that may mask configuration drift.
ansible.whyFlagged: The resources array in the template is empty or absent, meaning no infrastructure is deployed when this template is applied.
ansible.riskImpact: Empty templates deployed in automation pipelines may cause silent failures where expected security controls are never provisioned, creating gaps without alerts.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Ensure the resources array contains at least one resource definition. If the template is intentionally resource-free (e.g., a variables-only shared template), clearly document this intent and consider whether a different template structure is more appropriate.

ansible.name: ARM Template Location Default
ansible.description: The location parameter default value should be set to the resource group location to allow flexible deployment across regions.
ansible.summary: This finding means the location parameter uses a hardcoded region as default, which may deploy resources to an unintended or non-compliant region.
ansible.whyFlagged: The location parameter default is a hardcoded string (e.g., 'eastus') rather than the expression resourceGroup().location.
ansible.riskImpact: Hardcoded location defaults can deploy resources to regions that violate data residency requirements, compliance mandates, or organizational policies restricting specific geographies.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set the default value of the location parameter to resourceGroup().location (Bicep) or '[resourceGroup().location]' (ARM). This ensures resources deploy to the same region as their resource group unless explicitly overridden.

examples.bad:
// Bicep — hardcoded location default
param location string = 'eastus'
examples.good:
// Bicep — location defaults to resource group location
param location string = resourceGroup().location

references.name: Azure ARM Template Location Best Practices

ansible.name: ARM Template Location Parameter Type
ansible.description: The location parameter must be declared as the string type to correctly accept Azure region names.
ansible.summary: This finding means the location parameter uses an incorrect type, which can cause deployment failures or accept invalid location values.
ansible.whyFlagged: The location parameter type is not 'string', meaning it cannot correctly accept Azure region name values.
ansible.riskImpact: Incorrect parameter types can cause unpredictable deployment behavior or silently accept invalid location values, leading to resources being deployed to wrong or unintended regions.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Declare the location parameter with type 'string'. In Bicep: param location string = resourceGroup().location. Optionally restrict valid values using an @allowed() decorator listing permitted regions.

examples.bad:
// Bicep — location parameter with wrong type
param location array = []

ansible.name: ARM Template Resource Location Expression
ansible.description: Resource location properties should use a parameter expression or the value 'global', not a hardcoded region string.
ansible.summary: This finding means a resource has a hardcoded location value, preventing consistent multi-region deployments and potentially violating data residency policies.
ansible.whyFlagged: The location property of a resource is set to a hardcoded region string (e.g., 'westus2') instead of a parameter reference such as location or parameters('location').
ansible.riskImpact: Hardcoded locations cause resources to always deploy to a fixed region regardless of deployment parameters, violating data residency requirements and preventing legitimate geographic distribution or disaster recovery deployments.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Replace hardcoded location values with a reference to the location parameter: use 'location: location' in Bicep or '"location": "[parameters('location')]"' in ARM JSON. Reserve 'global' only for truly global resources such as Azure DNS zones.

ansible.name: ARM Template Use Location Parameter
ansible.description: Templates should use a location parameter rather than calling resourceGroup().location directly in resource definitions.
ansible.summary: This finding means resources reference resourceGroup().location inline instead of a centralized location parameter, making location overrides impossible for callers.
ansible.whyFlagged: Resource location properties call resourceGroup().location directly rather than referencing a parameter that defaults to resourceGroup().location.
ansible.riskImpact: When resources reference resourceGroup().location directly, callers cannot override the deployment location. This prevents compliant deployments in disaster recovery, multi-region, or geo-restricted scenarios.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Add a 'location' parameter with default value resourceGroup().location and reference it in all resource location properties. This maintains a sensible default while allowing callers to override the location at deployment time.

ansible.name: ARM Template Parameter Min/Max Values
ansible.description: Parameter minValue and maxValue constraints must be valid integers and minValue must be less than or equal to maxValue.
ansible.summary: This finding means a parameter's minValue or maxValue constraint is invalid, potentially allowing out-of-range inputs that bypass intended restrictions.
ansible.whyFlagged: A parameter has a minValue greater than maxValue, or the constraint values are not valid integers for the parameter's declared type.
ansible.riskImpact: Invalid min/max constraints may be silently bypassed, allowing out-of-range values to be passed. This could enable resource over-provisioning, quota exhaustion, or bypass of security-relevant numeric constraints such as allowed port ranges.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Ensure minValue is a valid integer less than or equal to maxValue for all integer parameters. Only apply minValue/maxValue to parameters of type 'int'. Validate constraint logic as part of deployment pipeline testing.

ansible.name: ARM Template Debug Deployment
ansible.description: Nested deployments must not use verbose debug detail levels that capture and log full HTTP request or response content.
ansible.summary: This finding means a nested deployment has debug logging enabled at a level that captures full request or response content, which may include secrets.
ansible.whyFlagged: A Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource has debugSetting.detailLevel set to 'RequestContent', 'ResponseContent', or 'All', logging full HTTP payloads that may contain sensitive data.
ansible.riskImpact: Debug logs with request/response content are stored in Azure deployment history in plain text. These logs may capture secrets, passwords, and access keys, which are accessible to any principal with read access to the resource group.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set debugSetting.detailLevel to 'None' on all nested Microsoft.Resources/deployments resources, or remove the debugSetting property entirely. Never use 'RequestContent', 'ResponseContent', or 'All' in production deployments.

ansible.name: ARM Template Parameter Data Types
ansible.description: Parameter default values must match the declared parameter type to prevent silent type coercion errors during deployment.
ansible.summary: This finding means a parameter's default value does not match its declared type, which can cause unpredictable deployment behavior.
ansible.whyFlagged: A parameter declares a type (e.g., 'int', 'bool') but its defaultValue is of a different type (e.g., a string '5' for an int parameter).
ansible.riskImpact: Type mismatches in default values can silently accept wrong inputs or cause cryptic deployment failures, making it harder to diagnose and correct insecure configurations.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Ensure each parameter's defaultValue matches its declared type. Use 0 for int defaults, true/false for bool, empty string ('') for string, and [] for array. In Bicep the compiler enforces this at build time.

examples.bad:
// Bicep — type mismatch: int parameter with string default
param retentionDays int = '30'  // String assigned to int

ansible.name: ARM Template Parameter Strong Type
ansible.description: Parameters that reference Azure-specific values should use strong types or allowed-value constraints to prevent invalid inputs.
ansible.summary: This finding means a parameter is missing strong type metadata or allowed-value constraints, allowing any string value to be passed without validation.
ansible.whyFlagged: Parameters for Azure locations, VM SKUs, or other enumerable Azure values are missing metadata.strongType hints or @allowed() constraints, bypassing IDE and toolchain validation.
ansible.riskImpact: Without strong type constraints, operators can pass any string value, increasing the risk of deploying to non-compliant regions, using deprecated SKUs, or referencing non-existent resources.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Use @allowed() decorators in Bicep to constrain parameters to a known set of valid values (e.g., permitted regions or SKUs). For ARM, add metadata.strongType to enable Azure Portal dropdowns and validation.

examples.bad:
// Bicep — unrestricted location parameter
param location string = resourceGroup().location  // Accepts any string

ansible.name: ARM Template Expression Length
ansible.description: ARM template expressions must not exceed the Azure-imposed maximum expression length to avoid deployment failures.
ansible.summary: This finding means a template expression exceeds the maximum length limit, which will cause the deployment to fail.
ansible.whyFlagged: A template expression exceeds the ARM engine's maximum supported expression length of 24,576 characters.
ansible.riskImpact: Expressions exceeding the limit cause deployment failures. Overly complex expressions also reduce maintainability and increase the likelihood of logic errors in security-relevant computations such as naming or RBAC assignments.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Refactor long expressions by splitting them into multiple intermediate variables in the 'variables' section and referencing those variables. Consider migrating complex expressions to Bicep, which produces more concise compiled ARM output.

ansible.name: ARM Template Parameter File Valid
ansible.description: ARM template parameter files must be valid JSON conforming to the parameter file schema.
ansible.summary: This finding means the parameter file contains malformed JSON or violates the parameter file schema, which can cause silent fallback to insecure default values.
ansible.whyFlagged: The parameter file is not valid JSON, or is missing required fields such as $schema, contentVersion, or the parameters object.
ansible.riskImpact: Invalid parameter files cause deployment failures or silent fallback to template default values, which may be insecure test-oriented defaults not suitable for production.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Ensure parameter files are valid JSON containing $schema (set to the parameter file schema URL), contentVersion, and a parameters object. Validate using 'az deployment group validate' or arm-ttk before every deployment.

ansible.name: ARM Template Parameter File HTTPS Scheme
ansible.description: ARM template parameter file schema URIs must use the HTTPS scheme rather than HTTP.
ansible.summary: This finding means the parameter file $schema URL uses HTTP, exposing toolchain schema validation to potential interception.
ansible.whyFlagged: The $schema property in the parameter file starts with 'http://' rather than 'https://'.
ansible.riskImpact: HTTP schema references in parameter files may be intercepted during toolchain validation, potentially allowing a malicious schema to suppress warnings or permit dangerous parameter values.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Change the $schema URL in the parameter file from 'http://' to 'https://'. Example: replace 'http://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2019-04-01/deploymentParameters.json#' with the https equivalent.

ansible.name: ARM Template Metadata Link
ansible.description: ARM template parameter files should include a metadata link pointing to the corresponding ARM template file.
ansible.summary: This finding means the parameter file is missing a metadata.template link, making it unclear which template this parameter file belongs to.
ansible.whyFlagged: The parameter file has no metadata.template property that links it back to its parent ARM template file.
ansible.riskImpact: Without a metadata link, operators or automation pipelines may pair the wrong parameter file with a template, silently applying incorrect security configurations to production deployments.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Add a metadata property with a template field to the parameter file pointing to the relative path of the corresponding ARM template. Example: add '"metadata": { "template": "../azuredeploy.json" }' at the top level of the parameter file.

ansible.name: ARM Template Parameter Value Set
ansible.description: Parameter files should provide explicit values for all template parameters rather than silently relying on template-defined defaults.
ansible.summary: This finding means the parameter file does not specify values for some parameters, which will cause the deployment to fall back to template default values that may be insecure.
ansible.whyFlagged: One or more parameters defined in the corresponding ARM template have no entry in the parameter file, meaning the deployment will use the template's default values.
ansible.riskImpact: Template default values are often set to permissive or test-oriented values. Silently falling back to defaults in production can result in insecure configurations such as wide-open NSG rules, disabled encryption, or development SKUs.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Provide explicit values for all parameters in the parameter file, even those that have safe-looking defaults. Use Azure Key Vault parameter references for all sensitive values. Review default values in templates periodically to ensure they remain secure.

references.name: Azure Key Vault in Parameter Files

ansible.name: ARM Template Use Comments
ansible.description: ARM template resource definitions should include a 'comments' property documenting the purpose of each resource.
ansible.summary: This finding means resource blocks in the ARM template lack comments, reducing auditability and slowing down security reviews.
ansible.whyFlagged: ARM template resource objects do not include a 'comments' field to explain their purpose, security role, or relationship to other resources.
ansible.riskImpact: Without comments, security reviewers and incident responders cannot quickly determine the intent of individual resources. This increases the time needed for security audits and the chance of overlooking misconfigured resources.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Add a 'comments' property to each resource object in ARM JSON templates. In Bicep, add inline // comments above each resource declaration explaining its security role and dependencies.

ansible.name: ARM Template Use Descriptions
ansible.description: Bicep resources, modules, and parameters should include @description() decorators to communicate purpose in the compiled ARM template.
ansible.summary: This finding means Bicep declarations are missing @description() decorators, so the compiled ARM template has no metadata descriptions for reviewers.
ansible.whyFlagged: Bicep resource, module, or parameter declarations do not have @description() decorators, resulting in generated ARM templates with no documentation metadata.
ansible.riskImpact: Without descriptions in the compiled template, operators relying on the ARM JSON cannot understand resource purposes, increasing the risk of misconfiguration during manual edits and slowing down security reviews.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Add @description() decorators to all Bicep resource, module, and parameter declarations. These compile into metadata.description fields in the generated ARM template and are also surfaced in the Azure Portal and tooling.

ansible.name: Deployment Output Secret Value
ansible.description: Deployment outputs must not expose secret or secure parameter values that would be visible in deployment history.
ansible.summary: This finding means a deployment output exposes a sensitive value such as a password, connection string, or key, making it visible in Azure deployment history to anyone with read access.
ansible.whyFlagged: The template outputs section references a securestring parameter, a Key Vault secret, or a resource property known to contain sensitive data (e.g., administratorLoginPassword, primaryKey).
ansible.riskImpact: Deployment outputs are stored in plain text in Azure deployment history indefinitely. Any principal with Reader access to the resource group can retrieve exposed secrets, leading to credential theft and potential full environment compromise.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Remove sensitive values from deployment outputs entirely. If a downstream resource needs the value, pass it as a secure parameter directly rather than routing it through an output. Mark any necessary output types as securestring to prevent storage in deployment history.

ansible.name: Deployment Admin Username Hardcoded
ansible.description: Administrator username properties must not be set from hardcoded or deterministic values; they must come from secure parameters.
ansible.summary: This finding means the template sets an administrator username from a hardcoded string or predictable expression, making it trivially discoverable by attackers.
ansible.whyFlagged: An administratorLogin or similar admin username property is set to a literal string (e.g., 'admin', 'adminUser') or a deterministic expression rather than a secure parameter supplied at deployment time.
ansible.riskImpact: Hardcoded admin usernames are easily discovered and used in brute-force, credential stuffing, and targeted attacks against management interfaces. Using known usernames like 'admin' or 'sa' significantly reduces the work factor for attackers.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Replace hardcoded admin usernames with a parameter decorated with @secure() (Bicep) or type securestring (ARM). Supply the value via a Key Vault reference in the parameter file or through a CI/CD pipeline secret. Avoid predictable usernames such as 'admin', 'administrator', 'root', or 'sa'.

ansible.name: Deployment Secure Value
ansible.description: Resource properties that hold sensitive values must be sourced from secure parameters, not plain string parameters or hardcoded literals.
ansible.summary: This finding means a secret property (password, key, connection string) is set from a non-secure parameter or literal, causing it to appear in plain text in deployment history.
ansible.whyFlagged: A property known to hold sensitive data (e.g., administratorLoginPassword, primarySharedKey) is assigned from a plain 'string' type parameter or a hardcoded literal instead of a @secure() parameter.
ansible.riskImpact: Plain string parameters are stored in Azure deployment history in clear text. Any principal with Reader access to the resource group can retrieve exposed secrets from deployment history, enabling unauthorized access to databases, storage, and other resources.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Mark all parameters that carry sensitive data with @secure() in Bicep or type securestring/secureObject in ARM. Supply values via Azure Key Vault parameter references in the deployment parameter file. Never embed secrets as literal values in templates or parameter files.

references.name: Azure Key Vault References in Parameters

ansible.name: Deployment Outer Secret Leak
ansible.description: Nested deployments must use inner scope expression evaluation to prevent secure parameter values from being evaluated in the parent context and logged.
ansible.summary: This finding means a nested deployment uses outer scope expression evaluation, causing secure parameters to be resolved in the parent deployment context where they may appear in logs.
ansible.whyFlagged: A Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource has expressionEvaluationOptions.scope set to 'Outer', or omits the property in a context that defaults to outer evaluation, allowing secure parameters to leak into the parent deployment history.
ansible.riskImpact: Outer scope evaluation resolves secure parameters in the parent deployment context. Resolved secret values may then appear in parent deployment logs and history in plain text, accessible to any principal with read access to the resource group.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Set expressionEvaluationOptions.scope to 'Inner' on all nested Microsoft.Resources/deployments resources. Inner scope ensures secure parameters are evaluated entirely within the nested deployment context and are never surfaced to the parent deployment history.

ansible.name: Deployment Secure Parameter
ansible.description: Parameters whose names or usage indicate they carry sensitive data must be declared as securestring or secureObject.
ansible.summary: This finding means the template contains parameters with names suggesting sensitive content (password, secret, key, token) that are not typed as secure parameters.
ansible.whyFlagged: Parameters with names matching patterns such as 'password', 'secret', 'key', 'token', 'credential', or 'connectionString' are declared as plain 'string' type rather than 'securestring'.
ansible.riskImpact: Plain string parameters are stored unredacted in Azure deployment history. Any principal with read access to the resource group can view these values, enabling credential theft and unauthorized access to resources provisioned by the template.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Declare all parameters holding sensitive data with @secure() in Bicep or type securestring/secureObject in ARM. Review all parameter names for indicators of sensitive content and audit existing deployment history to assess exposure of already-deployed templates.

ansible.name: Deployment Naming Requirements
ansible.description: Nested deployment resource names must meet Azure naming requirements: 1–64 characters, valid characters only, and must not end with a period.
ansible.summary: This finding means a nested deployment resource name violates Azure naming rules, which can cause deployment failures or naming conflicts in deployment history.
ansible.whyFlagged: The name of a Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource contains invalid characters, exceeds 64 characters, ends with a period, or is empty.
ansible.riskImpact: Invalid deployment names cause hard-to-diagnose deployment failures. Inconsistent naming also reduces auditability and makes it harder to trace security-relevant deployments through logs and history.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Ensure all nested deployment names are 1–64 characters, use only alphanumerics, underscores, parentheses, hyphens, and periods, and do not end with a period. Adopt a consistent naming convention such as 'deploy-<module>-<environment>' for easier auditing.

ansible.name: Deployment Secret Leak
ansible.description: All template parameters carrying sensitive data must be marked as secure to prevent secrets from being written to deployment history and logs.
ansible.summary: This finding means one or more parameters that receive sensitive values are not marked as secure, causing those values to be stored unredacted in Azure deployment history.
ansible.whyFlagged: The scanner identified parameters that receive sensitive values—based on name patterns or their assignment to sensitive resource properties—that are not typed as securestring or secureObject.
ansible.riskImpact: Azure deployment history retains non-secure parameter values in plain text for the lifetime of the deployment record. Compromised identities or overly permissive service principals with read access to the resource group can retrieve all exposed secrets, enabling lateral movement and resource takeover.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Audit all template parameters for sensitive content. Mark them with @secure() in Bicep or securestring/secureObject type in ARM. Rotate any credentials that were already passed as plain parameters in previous deployments. Use Azure Key Vault references for all production secrets. Consider running 'az deployment operation list' to review what has already been logged.

references.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1552.001: Credentials in Files
Azure Key Vault References in Parameters

ansible.name: Deployment Script Pinned URL
ansible.description: Deployment scripts that reference external script URLs must pin to a specific immutable version to prevent supply chain attacks.
ansible.summary: This finding means a deployment script resource loads an external script from an unpinned URL, making the deployment vulnerable to supply chain tampering.
ansible.whyFlagged: A Microsoft.Resources/deploymentScripts resource references an external script URL pointing to a mutable reference such as a 'main' branch, 'latest' tag, or floating URL that can be changed by a third party.
ansible.riskImpact: Deployment scripts run with managed identity permissions. An attacker who compromises the hosting endpoint (e.g., a GitHub repository or CDN) can inject malicious code that executes arbitrary Azure API calls, exfiltrates secrets, creates backdoor role assignments, or destroys resources.
ansible.remediationGuidance: Pin external script URLs to a specific immutable commit SHA or content hash. Prefer storing scripts in a private Azure Blob Storage container with a SAS token or using inline scripts via the scriptContent property to eliminate external URL dependencies entirely. Add URL integrity checks if external URLs must be used.

references.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1195: Supply Chain Compromise
